title: Rhetorical Synthesis
lead: This is the question type built from student notes. Synthesis means combining pieces of information into one statement that serves a purpose. In real writing you would read the sources, take notes, and draft the sentence yourself. On the SAT the reading and the note-taking are already done: you get the notes and a goal, and you choose the sentence that does the job. It is one of the most learnable types, because it depends less on reading skill and more on following a filter procedure exactly.

parts.title: Part 1 · What the question looks like
parts.html:
Every rhetorical synthesis question has the same four pieces.

PieceWhat it saysWhat to do with it
Introduction“While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:”Always the same. Skip it.
NotesSeveral bullet points of related facts about an unfamiliar topicRead second, looking only for what the goal needs.
Prompt“The student wants to [goal]. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?”Read first. Read only the goal; the question after it never changes.
ChoicesFour well-written sentencesTest each against the goal and the notes.

Most students start with the bullets because they come first. That is the mistake. The notes hold more information than you need, and without the goal you cannot tell which part matters. Read the goal before the notes.

parts.title: Part 2 · The two tests
parts.html:
Two mechanical skills decide these questions:

  • Goal-reading: turn the goal into a filter. “Emphasize the cost savings” means the right answer must put cost in the foreground. Every choice that does not is out, however well written and accurate.
  • Accuracy-checking: every note is a fact you must not distort. Choices contain small misstatements: a number shifted, a “may” turned into “will”, a comparison reversed.

The traps are predictable. One choice meets the goal but distorts a fact. Another is accurate but ignores the goal. A third is accurate and mentions the goal item without making it the point. The correct choice achieves the goal and uses the notes accurately.

parts.title: Part 3 · The method
parts.html:
1. Identify the goal and simplify it. The goal is stated plainly in the prompt. Cut it down to a word or two: “emphasize a difference between the two methods” becomes difference; “introduce the study and its findings” becomes study + findings.
  2. Read the notes for what is relevant. Look for the bullets that serve the goal. The relevant information may sit in one bullet or be spread across several.
  3. First pass: test each choice against the goal. Cross out every choice that does not do the job. The order matters. Students who check accuracy first get distracted by a choice whose facts are flawless but whose sentence ignores the goal.
  4. Second pass: test the survivors against the notes. Check numbers, dates, names and the strength of claims. “Can generate up to 40% savings” must not become “generates 40% savings”; the “up to” has to survive. “More efficient than X” must not become plain “efficient” or “more efficient than Y”. If a choice states something no bullet contains, it is out, even if it sounds plausible and supports the goal.

After both passes one choice is left: it accomplishes the goal and represents the notes accurately.

Tip. The goal verb is the answer's job description. Match the shape of the sentence to the job the verb describes.

parts.title: Part 4 · Worked example
parts.html:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • The novel David Copperfield by Charles Dickens focuses on the adventures of its title character, David Copperfield.
  • David Copperfield is considered a bildungsroman.
  • In a bildungsroman, the main character grows, learns, and changes from experience.
  • The novel Tom Jones by Henry Fielding focuses on the adventures of its title character, Tom Jones.
  • Tom Jones is considered a picaresque novel.
  • In a picaresque novel, the main character has many experiences but stays fundamentally the same.
The student wants to emphasize a similarity between the two novels. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal? A) David Copperfield and Tom Jones are both considered picaresque novels.
B) Both David Copperfield and Tom Jones focus on the adventures of their title characters.
C) David Copperfield was written by Charles Dickens; Tom Jones was written by Henry Fielding.
D) In David Copperfield, unlike in Tom Jones, the main character grows, learns, and changes from experience.

Goal, simplified: similarity.

Relevant notes: the notes give each novel a different type, a different author and a different kind of main character. The one thing they say about both is in bullets 1 and 4: each focuses on the adventures of its title character.

ChoicePass 1: goalPass 2: notes
AStates a similarityFails. Only Tom Jones is called picaresque. David Copperfield is a bildungsroman.
BStates a similarityAccurate: bullets 1 and 4
CFails. Two different authors is a difference.Not needed
DFails. “Unlike” signals a difference.Not needed

Notice the two kinds of wrong choice. C and D are true to the notes and miss the goal. A appears to meet the goal and misuses the notes. Only B passes both.

parts.title: Part 5 · The common goal types
parts.html:
GoalThe right answerWrong choices
Emphasize XPuts X in the main clause, often firstBury X in a side phrase (“while saving water, the garden thrives”) or omit it
Introduce a topic to an unfamiliar audienceDefines the topic in plain terms and assumes nothingDive into details or use jargon the audience would not know
Explain a drawback or concernStates the negative directly, with the reasonLead with the benefit and hide the drawback
Compare two itemsNames both items and the direction (more than, less than, similar to)Reverse the comparison or mention only one item
Present information from a specific sourceMatches that bullet exactly, including hedges like “researchers believe”Turn belief into proof

Two-part goals. Some goals ask for two things at once, such as “describe the study's method to an audience unfamiliar with the field”. The answer must do both: give the method and include the background a new reader needs. A choice that does only one part is wrong.

parts.title: Part 6 · Second worked example
parts.html:
Notes
  • Solar panels convert sunlight to electricity with no emissions during operation.
  • A typical home system costs $15,000 before incentives; tax credits can reduce the cost by up to 30%.
  • Panels typically lose about 0.5% of output per year.
  • Installation takes one to three days for most homes.
Goal. The student wants to emphasize that solar panel costs can be reduced.

Requirement. The sentence must make cost reduction its main point, not a side note.

ChoiceVerdict
A) Solar panels produce electricity with no emissions during operation, and installation typically takes one to three days.Accurate, but the goal is not addressed at all.
B) Solar panels lose only about 0.5% of output per year, which, along with tax credits of up to 30%, makes them a lasting investment.Mentions the tax credit in a side phrase. The main point is output, and “a lasting investment” is not in the notes.
C) While a typical home solar system costs $15,000 before incentives, tax credits can reduce that cost by up to 30%.Correct. The main clause is the cost reduction, and “can” and “up to 30%” are preserved.
D) Tax credits eliminate the cost of solar panel installation entirely.On the goal, but distorts the notes: up to 30%, not all of it.

This is the typical pattern: A fails the goal, B mentions it without emphasizing it, D fails accuracy, C does both.

Common mistake. Stopping the accuracy check at the numbers. Distortions hide in hedging words too: “can reduce” becoming “will reduce”, “up to 30%” becoming “30%”, “some researchers suggest” becoming “researchers have proven”. A trap choice keeps the numbers intact and changes the strength of the claim.

parts.title: Part 7 · Top tips
parts.html:
• Be strict. Do not reward a choice that “kind of” or “almost” meets the goal. Every part of the goal must be fully covered.
  • Ignore grammar and style. All four choices are correct, well-written sentences. Decide by the information they contain, not by how they sound.
  • Simplify the goal. A one-word test (“difference?”, “drawback?”) clears out choices quickly. You may need to go back to the notes to separate the last two.
  • Work in two passes. Goal first, accuracy second.
  • Skip what never changes. The introduction and the final question are identical every time. Read the goal and move on.

parts.title: Part 8 · Key words by goal
parts.html:
The goal in the question does most of the work, and a correct choice usually rewords the goal itself. Certain goals call for certain words, which makes the first pass very fast.

GoalThe correct choice will usually containCross out choices with
Emphasize a similarityboth, like, similarly, also, share, eachwhereas, unlike, however, but
Emphasize a difference or contrastwhereas, unlike, while, but, in contrastboth, like, similarly
Emphasize the variety, range or number of somethingSeveral examples, and words such as range, various, diverseOnly one example
Introduce a person or work to an unfamiliar audienceThe full name, and a phrase that says who or what it isA surname alone; a detail with no background
Present a study and its findingsThe study and what it foundMethod only, or result only
Give an example of somethingA specific case, namedA general statement about the topic

A general statement is not an example. If the goal is to show how wolves use body language, “Wolves communicate with one another in many ways” fails. It names the subject and gives no instance. “A wolf lowers its tail to show submission” passes.

“Unfamiliar audience” makes the answer longer. A reader who does not know the subject needs to be told what it is, so the correct choice usually carries a short description, and it is often the longest of the four.

This pass is about the goal. Keep the second pass from Part 3 as well: now and then a choice says exactly what the goal asks and gets a fact from the notes wrong, as choice A does in the worked example in Part 4.
